title: A Brief Look at The 7th Continent and the works of A. Merritt.
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ahyTF-4Agkg

Daniel (@dungeondive) opens with a reading from A. Merritt's *The Face in the Abyss* — a Harvard mining engineer, two shady companions and a map etched on a flexible sheet of gold — and that's the frame for his look at *The 7th Continent*. He rates Merritt the most important pulp writer of all, the prototype Lovecraft built on, and calls "The People of the Pit" (1918) one of the greatest short stories ever written.

The game's credits are dedicated to Gary Chalk, Joe Dever, Gary Gygax, Steve Jackson and Ian Livingstone, and Daniel takes that seriously: this is a Fighting Fantasy gamebook whose paragraphs live on the backs of cards, the map revealed rather than drawn. He still isn't sure why it isn't simply a lavishly produced book.

The rules are so lean that players suspect they're doing it wrong — one action a turn, draw from the stamina deck, count stars, and a curse on the second pass ends you. Easy to play, hard to win.

His reservation is the heart of the video. Exploration needs discovery and excitement; this nails the first and, unlike Warhammer Quest or Arkham Horror, never gets his pulse up. A game for a cup of tea, he says — and one that finally feels like reading Merritt.

----

Discovery without excitement: is a calm, cerebral exploration game a strength or a missing half? And which game has best captured pulp fiction for you?
